_doc: Knowledge overlay for data/chapter1_concept_graph_percpt_lp.json. Per concept: cues (code = Python regexes, words = lowercase phrases) used to identify the concept in a student prompt, and execution facts = what happens when the construct runs (the notional-machine facts that count as E2 evidence). DRAFT 2026-10-01: authored from each concept's description; to be reviewed by a teacher.

facts: The source file must be named after the public class it contains.
The compiler reads the source file; the text itself does not run.
A class declaration wraps all of the program's code inside braces.
If the public class name differs from the file name, the program does not compile.
When the program runs, the JVM starts executing at the first statement of main.
The program ends when main finishes its last statement.
Statements execute one after another, top to bottom.
Each statement ends with a semicolon; a missing semicolon is a compile error.
Braces group several statements so they execute together as one unit.
Variables declared inside a block exist only until the block ends.
print writes its argument to the console and leaves the cursor on the same line.
The next output after print continues on the same line.
println writes its argument and then moves the cursor to the next line.
The next output after println starts on a new line.
println() with no argument prints just a newline.
A string literal is printed exactly as written between the double quotes.
The quotes themselves are not printed.
javac translates the source code into bytecode without running it.
A syntax error stops compilation, so no bytecode is produced and nothing runs.
The java command loads the compiled bytecode into the JVM and executes main.
Runtime errors only appear when the program runs, after it compiled successfully.
A literal is a fixed value that evaluates to itself.
The form of a literal decides its type: 42 is an int, 3.14 is a double, 'a' is a char.
A primitive variable stores its value directly.
The type fixes which values a variable can hold and which operations apply.
An int holds whole numbers only; any fractional part is lost.
int arithmetic that goes past about 2.1 billion overflows and wraps around.
A double holds numbers with a fractional part.
double arithmetic can produce small rounding errors.
A boolean holds exactly one of two values: true or false.
Conditions in if statements and loops evaluate to a boolean.
A char holds a single character stored as a number code.
Arithmetic on a char uses its numeric code, so 'a' + 1 is 98.
A variable is a named storage location that holds one value at a time.
A local variable must be assigned before it is read, or the code does not compile.
Reading a variable gives its current value and does not change it.
The right side is evaluated first, then its value is stored in the variable on the left.
Assignment replaces the variable's old value with the new one.
After x = y, changing y later does not change x for primitive values.
An expression is evaluated to produce a single value.
Inner parts and method arguments are evaluated before the whole expression.
Arithmetic operators compute a new value from their operands.
% gives the remainder after division.
When both operands are int, / discards the fractional part of the result.
7 / 2 evaluates to 3 because both operands are integers.
Making one operand a double gives a fractional result.
A comparison operator evaluates to true or false.
For primitives, == compares the values; for objects, == compares references.
Multiplication and division are evaluated before addition and subtraction.
Operators of equal precedence are evaluated left to right.
Parentheses force their contents to be evaluated first.
A smaller type is widened automatically, so an int can be stored in a double.
Casting a double to int truncates the fractional part.
Narrowing conversions require an explicit cast.
A String variable holds a reference to a String object.
== on two Strings checks whether they are the same object, not whether they hold the same text.
.equals() compares the characters of the two Strings.
A String object cannot be changed; operations create a new String.
+ with a String operand converts the other operand to text and joins them into a new String.
+ is evaluated left to right, so 1 + 2 + "x" gives "3x" but "x" + 1 + 2 gives "x12".
A boolean expression evaluates to true or false.
A boolean expression can be used directly as a value without an if.
A relational operator compares two numbers and yields true or false.
< excludes the boundary value and <= includes it.
&& is true only when both sides are true.
|| is true when at least one side is true.
! flips true to false and false to true.
&& does not evaluate its right side when the left side is false.
|| does not evaluate its right side when the left side is true.
The condition is evaluated once; the body runs at most one time.
If the condition is false, the body is skipped and execution continues after it.
Exactly one of the two branches runs, depending on the condition.
The else branch runs only when the condition is false.
In an else-if chain the conditions are tested in order and only the first true branch runs.
An else attaches to the nearest unmatched if.
The condition is checked before every pass through the body.
The body repeats as long as the condition is true.
The loop ends when the condition becomes false.
The initialization runs once, before the first pass.
Before each pass the condition is checked; after each pass the update runs.
The loop ends when the condition becomes false.
The update must change the loop variable so the condition eventually becomes false.
If the condition never becomes false, the loop runs forever.
The bound and the comparison together decide how many passes happen.
The loop variable holds a different value on each pass.
The loop variable's value is what the condition tests.
i++ adds one to i.
x += 5 adds 5 to x and stores the result back in x.
The body's statements run once on every pass of the loop.
Changes made in one pass are visible in the next pass.
The accumulator is initialized once before the loop.
Each pass adds the current value to the accumulator.
After the loop the accumulator holds the total of all values.
The counter starts at zero before the loop.
The counter increases by one each time the tested condition holds.
After the loop the counter holds the number of matches.
The inner loop runs completely for every single pass of the outer loop.
The total number of inner passes is the outer count times the inner count.
A variable declared inside the loop body is created fresh on each pass.
A variable declared in the for header does not exist after the loop.
To use a value after the loop, declare the variable before the loop.
Declaring an array variable does not create an array; it holds no array yet.
The array type fixes the type of every element.
new int[n] allocates exactly n slots.
The size of an array is fixed when it is created and never grows.
New int and double slots start at 0, boolean slots at false, and object slots at null.
An initializer creates the array and fills it with the listed values in order.
The array's length equals the number of listed values.
a[i] accesses the element at position i, counting from 0.
The first element is a[0] and the last is a[a.length - 1].
a.length gives the number of slots in the array.
length is a field, written without parentheses.
Valid indices run from 0 to length minus 1.
Accessing an index outside that range throws an ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException at run time.
Using i <= a.length as a loop condition reads one slot past the end.
An index loop from 0 while i < a.length visits every element exactly once.
On each pass, a[i] is the element at the current index.
The for-each variable takes the value of each element in turn, not the index.
Assigning to the for-each variable does not change the array.
Assigning one array variable to another copies the reference, not the elements.
After b = a, a change through b is visible through a.
a[i][j] is element j of row i; each row is itself an array.
a.length is the number of rows and a[i].length is the length of row i.
Rows can have different lengths.
Command-line arguments arrive in args as Strings, in the order typed.
args[0] is the first argument after the class name.

words: convert the string to a number

facts: Integer.parseInt turns a String of digits into an int value.
Parsing text that is not a valid number throws a NumberFormatException.
Output is written to the console in the order the print statements execute.
Each read takes the next value from the input stream.
A value that has been read is consumed and cannot be read again.
StdDraw calls draw shapes on a canvas in the order they execute.
Input and output are sequences processed in order, one value after another.
The loop checks whether input remains before each read.
The loop ends when the input stream is empty.
< file makes the file's contents the program's standard input.
> file sends the program's standard output into the file.
A redirected file does not appear in args.
A pipe sends the first program's standard output into the second program's standard input.
The program reads the number of pages and then each link as a pair of page numbers.
Entry [i][j] is the probability of moving from page i to page j.
Each row of the transition matrix sums to 1.
Each count in a row is divided by the row total so the row sums to 1.
The division must be done in floating point or the probabilities become 0.
A random number between 0 and 1 is compared with running sums of the row's probabilities.
The next page is the first one whose running sum exceeds the random number.
Each pass of the loop moves the surfer to one next page.
The current page carries over from one pass to the next.
Each step adds one to the visit count of the current page.
Dividing the counts by the number of steps estimates each page's rank.
Repeatedly multiplying the probability vector by the transition matrix converges to the same ranks the simulation estimates.
